source_reviews.independent_solution: One object's action can change another object's velocity, deform it, or produce both effects. Starting, stopping, speed change, and direction change are velocity changes. Deformation changes the arrangement or dimensions of parts and need not remain after contact. These are possible effects, not a claim that every interaction always produces both or that continued motion alone proves a net force. This solution was saved before viewing options or author reasoning.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Force describes one object's action on another and is the cause of velocity change, not velocity itself, stored motion, or a continuing requirement for uniform motion. Another object's action can also alter relative motion of parts and deform the body. An idealized object with no subsequent other-body action retains its existing velocity after contact ends. Individual forces can exist without overall acceleration when balanced; that distinct real-world case is not the supplied no-other-action model.

source_reviews.independent_solution: A deforming action makes parts move non-rigidly relative to each other, changing their arrangement or distances and therefore the object's shape or dimensions. A spring compressed between hands shortens even if its center remains near rest. Common translation and rigid rotation preserve internal distances and are not deformation merely because absolute positions change. The frozen source solution preserves this relative-motion mechanism rather than the tautology that force causes deformation.
